## TL;DR

I removed the short, self-expiring overlap window from the cross-checkout heavy-slot test. Its fake Vitest processes now stay alive until the test releases them, so the test first observes the intended shared state (two running jobs and three queued jobs) and only then lets the processes exit. This makes the assertion independent of how quickly the machine starts five processes. No production behavior changed.

The reported 44-second failure in the release-profile check test did not reproduce. It completed in about 98 ms in the focused run, and the same test passed in 20 consecutive loaded repetitions and 20 consecutive repetitions without load. The task report records that evidence and does not assign an unverified cause to that incident.

## Work and rationale

The heavy-slot test launches five fake engineer commands across two fixture checkouts. The fake `vitest` executable previously appended a start line, slept for 200 ms, and appended an end line. The test inferred concurrency from those intervals while polling the shared log. That setup made the test’s evidence depend on scheduling: if a worker was descheduled or process startup was delayed, the fixed overlap window could expire before the test reliably observed the expected concurrency. The test also treated the run log as its source of truth for peak concurrency, mixing the behavior under test with timing of log writes and polling.

I changed the fixture to give each fake process a shared release-file path. A child records its start and waits until that file exists. The parent waits for the cross-process slot registry to report exactly two running jobs and three queued jobs, then creates the release file. All jobs can then finish normally. This keeps the real behavior under test—the slot limiter and queue across two independent checkouts—while replacing the short time window with an explicit event controlled by the test. The existing bounded wait remains only as a deadlock guard: if child processes fail to start or the limiter stops progressing, the test exits with an actionable failure instead of hanging indefinitely. The timeout is not being used as evidence that the concurrency behavior happened.

The change is confined to the test fixture in `src/ui-app/tests/engineer-resources.test.ts`. The release-profile check test exercises `cmdCheck`, a real shell command (`false`), and the check-run history persistence path. It contains no narrow custom deadline, and its test framework timeout is not what the focused run approached. I did not mock the command runner or persistence layer because doing so would stop testing the behavior named by that case. There was no observed reason to alter that test or production code.

## Approaches tried

I first ran both complete test files together. All selected tests passed, including the heavy-slot test (about 1.6 seconds) and the release-profile test (about 98 ms). This did not reproduce either reported failure. I then replaced the 200 ms fake-job lifetime with an explicit release-file handshake and retained a 15-second bounded wait for the expected slot state. The test case timeout is 30 seconds to allow process startup and cleanup under load; the assertion is driven by the slot-state event, not by consuming that time budget.

For repetition, I ran the two named cases 20 consecutive times with a CPU-bound background process and then 20 consecutive times without that load. Every invocation passed. I used a finite, explicitly tracked process and stopped it with its PID after the loaded batch. These runs establish that the revised fixture behaves consistently in the conditions reproduced here. They do not prove what caused the original 44-second incident because that behavior did not recur.

Finally, I ran `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check`. The remote changed-path validation passed its build and scoped tests; local format/lint, build, UI checks, contrast audit, and remaining selected checks passed. The check reported “All checks passed.”

## Challenges and blockers

The principal diagnostic limitation is that the original full-release machine load and its exact runtime/process state were not available to recreate. In this session the release-profile test repeatedly completed quickly, including during the CPU-bound batch. The task description says it was recorded as failed after 44 seconds, but that alone does not distinguish a test timeout from delayed process startup, a host-level pause, or another transient environmental condition. I therefore cannot truthfully claim a reproduced root cause for that incident.

The load repetition is a deliberate CPU stress approximation, not a recreation of the release host’s exact memory pressure, disk contention, runner state, or concurrent suite activity. It gives direct evidence that the old short concurrency window has been removed from the heavy-slot fixture, while leaving the unexplained release-profile timing as a documented limitation for future triage if it recurs.

## Key learnings

Concurrency tests that model several processes should control when fake work completes. A short sleep can create an overlap in the usual case, but it couples the assertion to scheduling and host load. Holding fake work behind an explicit release event makes the relevant state observable before completion and keeps a bounded timeout in its proper role as a hang guard.

A single fast reproduction is not enough to explain a historical long-duration test failure. The release-profile case passed 40 repeated runs here, so changing its timeout or weakening its assertions would have hidden uncertainty rather than fixed demonstrated behavior. If the 44-second failure recurs, the next useful evidence is the actual Vitest timeout/error text and timing around command spawn, command close, and check-store recording on that run.
